You lower your eyes to the book. Seraphel doesn’t try to reopen the exchange. She takes a slim collection of poems from the side table and reads in the neighboring chair while the card game continues across the room.

The chapter uses *concordance* in a technical sense. It is the work of translating an obligation between magical traditions without accidentally changing what either party has promised.

A fae agreement depends upon consent and exact terms. An angelic oath may depend upon ritual witness and moral certainty. A demon compact can pledge life force; an elven boundary may remain active long after its makers die. Identical words do not necessarily create identical obligations.

Human arbiters were valued because they could learn limited fragments of several traditions. The book is careful to say this did not grant mastery. It allowed them to recognize when two parties believed they had agreed while their magic enforced different promises.

One example concerns a dragon’s grant of “temporary” mining rights. The dragon intended permission lasting until her death; the human merchants understood a term of twelve years. Arbitration required no spell from the human mediator—only a translation precise enough for both sides to consent to the same duration.

In the margin, someone has written:

*This could have been prevented by asking the dragon what temporary meant.*

The common room gradually quiets around you. Dena’s two friends depart with most of the wine. Dena stays for one final hand, wins Rashid’s collar stud, and announces that he may buy it back by remembering his schedule next time. Thessaly insists upon counting the deck before anyone leaves.

Ysolde returns from the garden with cold clinging to her clothes. Aldric comes back from the chapel shortly afterward. Neither disturbs the readers by the fire.

You continue to the chapter’s final section. It describes the human seat’s authority as persuasive rather than sovereign: an arbitrator cannot compel agreement, only expose the points at which agreement has failed. The parties must still choose new terms.

The final paragraph warns that human adaptability was never the same as neutrality. Human arbiters possessed loyalties, appetites, and political interests of their own; their rulings required the same scrutiny as any other seat’s decisions.

By the time you reach the last line, the fire has settled into a red glow. Seraphel has finished several pages of her own book without speaking.

The next chapter begins on the facing page:

*SUCCESSION, RECOGNITION, AND CHALLENGES TO A SEAT.*
